warmup.q: A batch job wrote 500,000 idempotency keys with EX 3. Three seconds later a client sends GET idem:250000. What does it get, and is the key's memory free yet?
options: The old value: Redis deletes expired keys only once a second, in a sweep
nil, and the memory of all 500,000 keys is already free
nil, but most of the 500,000 keys are still in memory for about another second
nil only after SCAN has visited the key
warmup.why: Every command checks a key's deadline before it runs, so the GET deletes that one key and answers nil. The other keys are removed by a cycle that runs 10 times a second in slices of at most 25 ms. On the lab server it needed about 1.1 seconds to reclaim all 500,000. There is no once-a-second sweep that could return a stale value, and SCAN plays no part.

sections.h: A TTL is a deadline Redis keeps with the key
sections.html:
Lessons 3 and 4 were about what a key costs. This lesson is about how a cache forgets, which every cache must: by deadline, when a key's time is up, and by choice, when memory runs out. Start with the deadline. An idempotency key protects one card payment from being charged twice. Your service stores idem:7f3a when the request arrives, and a client that retries within the next 24 hours finds it and gets the first answer back. After that the key is garbage. At 35 payments a second, that is 3 million new keys a day.

Without help from the server you would clean up yourself: store the creation time inside each value, and run a job that walks every key with SCAN (lesson 3's page-by-page cursor) and deletes the old ones. That job reads 3 million keys a day on lesson 2's single thread (the one thread that runs every command, one at a time), and any key it misses stays forever.

So Redis lets you give a key a deadline. SET idem:7f3a pending EX 86400 stores the value and says "delete this 86,400 seconds from now". Redis turns that into an absolute time, a Unix timestamp in milliseconds, and keeps it with the key. It also keeps a second index that holds only the keys that have a deadline, and INFO keyspace shows both counts: keys=2,expires=1. The time a key has left is its TTL, time to live. TTL reports it in seconds, PTTL in milliseconds, and EXPIRETIME returns the deadline itself.

That picture is the model for this lesson. Redis gets rid of keys in two ways. Expiry removes keys whose deadline has passed. Eviction removes keys that Redis chooses itself when memory is full. Both run on the same single thread, between and before your commands, and the rest of the lesson fills in how.

A few rules cause most TTL bugs:

  • A plain SET replaces the value and drops the TTL, so the key now lives forever. Add KEEPTTL (Redis 6.0) to keep the old deadline. Commands that change a value in place, such as INCR, HSET or RPUSH, keep it.
  • EXPIRE on a key that already has a TTL replaces the deadline. Since Redis 7.0 it takes NX (only if there is no TTL yet), XX (only if there is one), GT (only if the new deadline is later) and LT (only if it is earlier).
  • PERSIST removes the TTL. TTL answers -1 for a key without one, and -2 for a key that doesn't exist.
  • A TTL belongs to a whole key. To expire single fields of a hash, Redis 7.4 added HEXPIRE, and Valkey 9.0 added the same family of commands.

try.title: Set, keep and lose a TTL
steps: From the labs folder, start the server if it isn't running (docker compose -f env/redis.yml up -d) and open a prompt with docker compose -f env/redis.yml exec redis redis-cli.
Type the commands below one at a time. Before the second TTL idem:7f3a, predict what a plain SET did to the deadline.
Before each EXPIRE ... GT and EXPIRE ... NX, predict whether it changes anything. It returns 1 when it did and 0 when it didn't.

try.expect: The first TTL prints (integer) 86400 and PTTL about (integer) 86399999. After the plain SET idem:7f3a done, TTL prints (integer) -1: the key now lives forever. SET ... KEEPTTL keeps the deadline, so the next TTL is back near 86400. INCR keeps the 60-second TTL that EXPIRE set, so TTL auths:card:7 still prints (integer) 60. EXPIRE ... 30 GT returns (integer) 0 (30 s is not later than 60 s) and EXPIRE ... 600 GT returns (integer) 1. EXPIRE ... NX returns 0 because the key already has a TTL. After PERSIST, TTL is -1; for a missing key it is -2. INFO keyspace ends with db0:keys=2,expires=1,...: two keys, one of them in the expires index.

sections.h: Expired keys die on access, and by sampling
sections.html:
The 3 million idempotency keys from the last section each have their own deadline, somewhere in the next 24 hours, and Redis has to delete each one at about the right moment, on one thread.

The obvious design is a timer per key. Three million timers cost memory, and they would all fire on the one thread. The next idea is a sweep: once a second, check every key that has a deadline. That is 3 million comparisons every second, and while the sweep runs no client is served, because it runs on the same thread as every command.

Redis does two cheap things instead.

The first is lazy expiry. Every command that touches a key checks the key's deadline first. If the deadline has passed, Redis deletes the key right there and behaves as if it had never existed. That costs one comparison per access, and it guarantees that no client ever reads an expired value. On its own it leaks memory: most idempotency keys are written once and never read again, so nothing would ever look at them.

The second is active expiry, a cycle on the main thread. Ten times a second (the hz setting, 10 by default), it walks the expires index from where it stopped last time, checks 20 keys and deletes the expired ones. If more than 10% of that batch had expired, there is probably more to do, so it takes another batch at once. It stops when a batch comes back mostly clean, or when it has used 25 ms, a quarter of the 100 ms between runs. A few expired keys cost almost nothing. Many get the thread's full attention, in slices short enough that clients are still served in between.

So an expired key becomes invisible at once, and leaves memory a little later. The lab server showed both with 500,000 idempotency keys that shared one deadline. A GET returned nil in the first poll after the deadline, and that GET deleted exactly one key: the expired count went from 0 to 1 while DBSIZE still said 500,001. The cycle then removed about 400,000 keys a second, and memory fell from 40 MB to 2 MB in about 1.1 seconds. Those deletions are main-thread work, so a mass expiry is a latency bump for every client. Lesson 6 shows how to spread deadlines out.

INFO stats keeps the score: expired_keys counts every expiry, expired_keys_active the cycle's share, and expired_time_cap_reached_count the runs that hit the 25 ms limit. Replicas never expire keys on their own. They wait for the primary to send a DEL (lesson 9), and until it arrives they answer reads for an expired key with nil, like the primary.

sections.h: With a maxmemory limit, a full Redis refuses writes by default
sections.html:
Expiry only removes keys that have a deadline. A cache whose entries have no TTL, or a write rate that outruns the TTLs, keeps growing. By default nothing stops it: on 64-bit systems maxmemory is 0, which means no limit. Redis grows until it reaches the memory limit of its container or VM, and then the Linux kernel's out-of-memory killer ends the process. In Docker you see exit code 137. Every client loses its connection at once, and a Redis without persistence comes back empty.

The fix is to give Redis a budget: maxmemory 4gb in the config file, or CONFIG SET maxmemory 4gb while it runs. Before Redis runs a command that can add data (SET, HSET, LPUSH, INCR and many more), it compares its memory use with the limit. Under the limit, the command runs. Over it, the eviction policy decides what happens.

The default policy is noeviction: refuse the write with an error and keep every key. The lab's small server has a 4 MB limit and already uses 1.41 MB when it is empty. About 2,300 values of 1 KB fit, and then the next write fails:

(error) OOM command not allowed when used memory > 'maxmemory'.

Reads keep working, and so do DEL and UNLINK. Refusing writes is the right default for data you can't afford to lose. If idempotency keys disappeared without a word, a retried payment would be charged twice. An error at least pages someone.

Two details about the number. The check runs before each command, so the command itself can push memory past the limit: in one run the lab server stopped at 4,218,576 bytes against a limit of 4,194,304. A single command that builds a big value, such as SUNIONSTORE over two large sets, can overshoot by far more. And maxmemory is compared with what the memory allocator handed out (used_memory), not with what the kernel charges the process (used_memory_rss, which includes fragmentation). The buffers that feed replicas and the append-only file (Redis's on-disk log of writes, lesson 9) aren't counted at all, and a background save can need extra memory too (lesson 9). So set maxmemory well below the container's limit, and graph both numbers.

sections.h: Eviction is a bet on the future, and LRU is only one bet
sections.html:
When memory is full, a cache has to guess which key it will need least soon. Lesson 1 found two places where LRU guesses badly: a loop just longer than the cache defeats it completely, and under skew it spends slots on keys that never come back. Every eviction policy answers the same question with different evidence.

FIFO evicts the key inserted first and ignores use entirely. Its bookkeeping is one queue, and it throws hot keys out on schedule. LRU evicts the key unused for longest. It holds hot keys well under skew, and it breaks three ways. A one-time scan, such as a nightly report that reads every key once, makes every scanned key look recent and pushes the hot keys out. Every hit is a write to shared state, a list move under a lock, so threads queue on that lock. And a key asked for once travels the whole list before it leaves. LFU evicts the key with the fewest hits. A scan adds one hit to each key, so it can't push out keys with hundreds, but the counts must decay, or yesterday's hot key stays forever.

Newer policies mix the evidence. ARC (IBM, 2003) keeps one list for keys seen once and one for keys seen again, remembers the names of keys it recently evicted, and shifts space between the two lists whenever a remembered key comes back. On a scan-heavy database benchmark with a 4 GB cache it hit 20% of requests where LRU hit 9.19%. W-TinyLFU, the policy in Caffeine, the JVM cache library, puts a small LRU window in front of the main cache. A key leaving the window gets in only if a Count-min sketch (lesson 4), costing about 8 bytes per entry, says it is used more often than the key it would push out.

The newest results come from counting one-hit wonders, keys requested once and never again. Across 6,594 production traces, the S3-FIFO paper (2023) found a median of 26% one-hit wonders per trace, and 72% within any stretch of a trace that touched 10% of its keys. So drop new keys quickly unless they prove themselves. S3-FIFO puts new keys in a small FIFO that holds 10% of the cache, and moves only keys requested again while there into the main FIFO. Keys it drops leave their names in a ghost queue, and a returning name skips the small queue. It had the lowest average miss ratio on 10 of its 14 datasets, and on 16 threads it served six times the requests of a well-tuned LRU, because a hit only bumps a 2-bit counter. SIEVE (2024) keeps one FIFO list and one visited bit per key. A hit sets the bit and moves nothing. To evict, a hand walks from the oldest key toward the newest, clears the bits it finds set, and evicts the first key whose bit is clear. Keys the hand spares stay where they are, and a new key that isn't requested again goes the first time the hand reaches it. On Zipf traffic with α = 1 its authors measured 13 to 18% fewer misses than LRU, at twice LRU's throughput on 16 threads. It is a close cousin of the clock sweep from the Storage track's lesson on the buffer pool.

No Docker needed. */ public class PolicyDemo { interface Policy { boolean access(int key); } public static void main(String[] args) { int n = 100_000; int[] zipf = zipfTrace(n, 1.0, 1_000_000, 7); int[] scans = withScans(zipf, n); System.out.println("miss ratio on the Zipf requests (alpha 1.0, 100,000 keys)"); System.out.println("cache workload FIFO LRU SIEVE"); for (int size : new int[] {1_000, 10_000}) { for (int[] trace : new int[][] {zipf, scans}) { System.out.printf("%,6d %-12s %6.1f%% %5.1f%% %5.1f%%%n", size, trace == zipf ? "Zipf" : "Zipf + scans", 100 * missRatio(trace, new Fifo(size), n), 100 * missRatio(trace, new Lru(size), n), 100 * missRatio(trace, new Sieve(size), n)); } } } /** Misses among the Zipf requests after a warm-up; scan keys (above n) are replayed but not counted. */ static double missRatio(int[] trace, Policy policy, int n) { long counted = 0, misses = 0; for (int i = 0; i < trace.length; i++) { boolean hit = policy.access(trace[i]); if (i >= trace.length / 5 && trace[i] <= n) { counted++; if (!hit) misses++; } } return (double) misses / counted; } /** FIFO: evict the key that was inserted first; a hit changes nothing. */ static final class Fifo implements Policy { final int capacity; final ArrayDeque<Integer> queue = new ArrayDeque<>(); final Set<Integer> cached = new HashSet<>(); Fifo(int capacity) { this.capacity = capacity; } public boolean access(int key) { if (cached.contains(key)) return true; if (cached.size() >= capacity) cached.remove(queue.pollFirst()); queue.addLast(key); cached.add(key); return false; } } /** LRU: a hit moves the key to the newest end; evict from the oldest end. */ static final class Lru implements Policy { final Map<Integer, Boolean> map; Lru(int capacity) { map = new LinkedHashMap<>(16, 0.75f, true) { @Override protected boolean removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry<Integer, Boolean> eldest) { return size() > capacity; } }; } public boolean access(int key) { if (map.get(key) != null) return true; map.put(key, Boolean.TRUE); return false; } } /** SIEVE: one FIFO list and a visited bit. A hit only sets the bit; the hand evicts the first unvisited key. */ static final class Sieve implements Policy { static final class Node { final int key; boolean visited; Node newer, older; Node(int key) { this.key = key; } } final int capacity; final Map<Integer, Node> nodes = new HashMap<>(); Node head, tail, hand; // head: newest, tail: oldest Sieve(int capacity) { this.capacity = capacity; } public boolean access(int key) { Node node = nodes.get(key); if (node != null) { node.visited = true; // no move, no lock needed in a concurrent version return true; } if (nodes.size() >= capacity) evict(); node = new Node(key); // new keys always enter at the head node.older = head; if (head != null) head.newer = node; head = node; if (tail == null) tail = node; nodes.put(key, node); return false; } void evict() { Node o = hand != null ? hand : tail; while (o.visited) { // spare visited keys, clear their bit, keep walking o.visited = false; o = o.newer != null ? o.newer : tail; // past the head: start again from the tail } hand = o.newer; // the next eviction resumes here if (o.newer != null) o.newer.older = o.older; else head = o.older; if (o.older != null) o.older.newer = o.newer; else tail = o.newer; nodes.remove(o.key); } } /** After every 50,000 requests, a one-time scan of 5,000 keys nobody asks for again. */ static int[] withScans(int[] zipf, int n) { int[] out = new int[zipf.length + zipf.length / 50_000 * 5_000]; int next = n + 1, j = 0; for (int i = 0; i < zipf.length; i++) { out[j++] = zipf[i]; if ((i + 1) % 50_000 == 0) for (int s = 0; s < 5_000; s++) out[j++] = next++; } return out; } static int[] zipfTrace(int n, double alpha, int length, long seed) { double[] cdf = new double[n]; double total = 0; for (int k = 1; k <= n; k++) total += Math.pow(k, -alpha); double running = 0; for (int k = 1; k <= n; k++) { running += Math.pow(k, -alpha) / total; cdf[k - 1] = running; } cdf[n - 1] = 1.0; Random random = new Random(seed); int[] trace = new int[length]; for (int i = 0; i < length; i++) { int k = Arrays.binarySearch(cdf, random.nextDouble()); trace[i] = (k >= 0 ? k : -k - 1) + 1; } return trace; } }

No Docker needed. */ fun main() { val n = 100_000 val zipf = zipfTrace(n, 1.0, 1_000_000, 7) val scans = withScans(zipf, n) println("miss ratio on the Zipf requests (alpha 1.0, 100,000 keys)") println("cache workload FIFO LRU SIEVE") for (size in listOf(1_000, 10_000)) { for ((name, trace) in listOf("Zipf" to zipf, "Zipf + scans" to scans)) { println("%,6d %-12s %6.1f%% %5.1f%% %5.1f%%".format(size, name, 100 * missRatio(trace, Fifo(size), n), 100 * missRatio(trace, Lru(size), n), 100 * missRatio(trace, Sieve(size), n))) } } } private interface Policy { fun access(key: Int): Boolean } /** Misses among the Zipf requests after a warm-up; scan keys (above n) are replayed but not counted. */ private fun missRatio(trace: IntArray, policy: Policy, n: Int): Double { var counted = 0L var misses = 0L trace.forEachIndexed { i, key -> val hit = policy.access(key) if (i >= trace.size / 5 && key <= n) { counted++ if (!hit) misses++ } } return misses.toDouble() / counted } /** FIFO: evict the key that was inserted first; a hit changes nothing. */ private class Fifo(val capacity: Int) : Policy { private val queue = ArrayDeque<Int>() private val cached = HashSet<Int>() override fun access(key: Int): Boolean { if (key in cached) return true if (cached.size >= capacity) cached.remove(queue.removeFirst()) queue.addLast(key) cached.add(key) return false } } /** LRU: a hit moves the key to the newest end; evict from the oldest end. */ private class Lru(val capacity: Int) : Policy { private val map = object : LinkedHashMap<Int, Boolean>(16, 0.75f, true) { override fun removeEldestEntry(eldest: MutableMap.MutableEntry<Int, Boolean>) = size > capacity } override fun access(key: Int): Boolean { if (map[key] != null) return true map[key] = true return false } } /** SIEVE: one FIFO list and a visited bit. A hit only sets the bit; the hand evicts the first unvisited key. */ private class Sieve(val capacity: Int) : Policy { private class Node(val key: Int) { var visited = false var newer: Node? = null var older: Node? = null } private val nodes = HashMap<Int, Node>() private var head: Node? = null // newest private var tail: Node? = null // oldest private var hand: Node? = null override fun access(key: Int): Boolean { nodes[key]?.let { it.visited = true // no move, no lock needed in a concurrent version return true } if (nodes.size >= capacity) evict() val node = Node(key) // new keys always enter at the head node.older = head head?.newer = node head = node if (tail == null) tail = node nodes[key] = node return false } private fun evict() { var o = hand ?: tail!! while (o.visited) { // spare visited keys, clear their bit, keep walking o.visited = false o = o.newer ?: tail!! // past the head: start again from the tail } hand = o.newer // the next eviction resumes here if (o.newer != null) o.newer!!.older = o.older else head = o.older if (o.older != null) o.older!!.newer = o.newer else tail = o.newer nodes.remove(o.key) } } /** After every 50,000 requests, a one-time scan of 5,000 keys nobody asks for again. */ private fun withScans(zipf: IntArray, n: Int): IntArray { val out = ArrayList<Int>(zipf.size + zipf.size / 10) var next = n + 1 zipf.forEachIndexed { i, key -> out += key if ((i + 1) % 50_000 == 0) repeat(5_000) { out += next++ } } return out.toIntArray() } private fun zipfTrace(n: Int, alpha: Double, length: Int, seed: Long): IntArray { val total = (1..n).sumOf { it.toDouble().pow(-alpha) } var running = 0.0 val cdf = DoubleArray(n) { running += (it + 1.0).pow(-alpha) / total; running } cdf[n - 1] = 1.0 val random = Random(seed) return IntArray(length) { val k = cdf.binarySearch(random.nextDouble()) (if (k >= 0) k else -k - 1) + 1 } }

With the scans at 10,000 slots, FIFO rose to 32.2% and LRU to 29.0%, while SIEVE stayed at 21.6%: scan keys enter unvisited, so the hand evicts them before any key that was hit. At 1,000 slots the scans changed little for any policy. A key the hand spares keeps its place in the list with its bit cleared, while LRU moves a key on every hit. sections.h: Eviction picks its victim from a small random sample
sections.html:
So which of these does Redis use? None of them exactly. A cache is allowed to lose entries (a missing card-issuer response only means one slow call to the issuer), so for a cache you want Redis to make room instead of refusing, and to choose well. But Redis can't afford the bookkeeping most policies need. Exact LRU keeps every key in a linked list and moves a key on every access: two pointers, 16 bytes, per key, plus a list update on every read. With 50 million keys that is 800 MB of pointers, rewritten on the hot path of the one thread that runs every command.

So Redis samples. Every key's header has 24 bits for the time of its last access, counted in seconds. When Redis must free memory, it picks 5 keys at random (maxmemory-samples), adds them to a pool of the 16 best candidates it has seen so far, and evicts the one that has been idle longest. It repeats until memory is under the limit. Old keys collect in the pool across rounds, so the result is close to true LRU, and 10 samples gets closer still. The lesson's demo keeps 200 hot keys and reads them before each of four batches of 800 keys that are written once and never read. Under allkeys-random, 79 of the 200 hot keys were evicted in one run. Under allkeys-lru, all 200 survived and most of the oldest batch was gone.

Redis's LFU (since 4.0) reuses the same 24 bits: 16 for when the counter last decayed, in minutes, and 8 for a logarithmic counter. Each hit raises the counter with a probability that shrinks as it grows, so about a million hits take it to its maximum, 255, and it drops by one for every minute nobody touches the key. A new key starts at 5, so it gets a chance before it is judged, and a scan adds at most one point to each key it reads. LRM, least recently modified (Redis 8.6), updates a key's stamp only on writes, so a key that is read all day but never changed can still go. None of the newer policies from the last section is in Redis 8.10; the SIEVE authors list Dragonfly among the systems that adopted SIEVE.

Every policy comes as allkeys-*, which considers every key, or volatile-*, which considers only keys with a TTL. A volatile-* policy on a server with no TTL keys behaves exactly like noeviction. volatile-ttl evicts the key nearest its deadline. For a cache, start with allkeys-lru, or allkeys-lfu when a few keys are very hot and scans happen. For data, use noeviction. Keep the two in separate Redis instances.

frames.say: Keys that are read all the time keep resetting their stamp to idle 0, so any older candidate beats them. A hot key can only go when a whole sample, and the pool, hold nothing older, which is rare. In the demo, allkeys-lru kept all 200 hot keys, while allkeys-random lost 79 of them. One catch: the stamp counts whole seconds, so keys touched in the same second tie.

try.title: Compare LRU, random and LFU on the same load
steps: With the small server still running, run EvictionDemo three times from the labs folder, with -Pargs=allkeys-lru, -Pargs=allkeys-random and -Pargs=allkeys-lfu. Each run takes about 5 seconds: the demo waits a second between batches, because the LRU clock only moves once a second.
Before each run, predict how many of the 200 hot keys survive, and which cold batch loses the most.

After the allkeys-lfu run, open the small server's prompt and compare OBJECT FREQ hot:1 with OBJECT FREQ cold:3:5. Then try -Pargs=volatile-lru: no key has a TTL. When you are done, stop both servers and delete their data: docker compose -f env/redis.yml --profile small down -v.

code.title: EvictionDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.cache.l05.demo import redis.clients.jedis.RedisClient import redis.clients.jedis.exceptions.JedisDataException /** * Fills the tiny lab server (port 6380, maxmemory 4mb) under one eviction policy and reports what survived. * 200 hot keys are read before every batch; four batches of 800 cold keys are written once and never read. * It empties that server first, so never point it at a Redis you care about. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val policy = args.firstOrNull() ?: "allkeys-lru" val value = "x".repeat(1_000) RedisClient.builder().hostAndPort("localhost", 6380).build().use { redis -> redis.flushAll() redis.configSet("maxmemory-policy", policy) val evictedBefore = redis.stat("stats", "evicted_keys") println("policy $policy, maxmemory ${redis.stat("memory", "maxmemory")} bytes") val hot = (0 until 200).map { "hot:$it" } hot.forEach { redis.set(it, value) } for (round in 0 until 4) { Thread.sleep(1_100) // let the once-a-second LRU clock move hot.forEach { redis.get(it) } // read the hot keys: they are young again var written = 0 var error: String? = null for (i in 0 until 800) { try { redis.set("cold:$round:$i", value) written++ } catch (e: JedisDataException) { error = e.message break } } println("batch ${round + 1}: wrote $written cold keys" + (error?.let { ", then: $it" } ?: "")) if (error != null) break } val hotLeft = hot.count { redis.exists(it) } val cold = (0 until 4).map { round -> (0 until 800).count { redis.exists("cold:$round:$it") } } println("hot keys left: $hotLeft of 200") println("cold keys left per batch: ${cold.joinToString(", ")}") println("evicted_keys: ${redis.stat("stats", "evicted_keys") - evictedBefore}, used_memory: ${redis.stat("memory", "used_memory")}") } } private fun RedisClient.stat(section: String, field: String): Long = info(section).lineSequence().map { it.trim() }.first { it.startsWith("$field:") }.substringAfter(':').toLong()

alt.html: package sfz.cache.l05.demo; import redis.clients.jedis.RedisClient; import redis.clients.jedis.exceptions.JedisDataException; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** * Fills the tiny lab server (port 6380, maxmemory 4mb) under one eviction policy and reports what survived. * 200 hot keys are read before every batch; four batches of 800 cold keys are written once and never read. * It empties that server first, so never point it at a Redis you care about. */ public class EvictionDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { String policy = args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "allkeys-lru"; String value = "x".repeat(1_000); try (RedisClient redis = RedisClient.builder().hostAndPort("localhost", 6380).build()) { redis.flushAll(); redis.configSet("maxmemory-policy", policy); long evictedBefore = stat(redis, "stats", "evicted_keys"); System.out.println("policy " + policy + ", maxmemory " + stat(redis, "memory", "maxmemory") + " bytes"); List<String> hot = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < 200; i++) { hot.add("hot:" + i); redis.set("hot:" + i, value); } for (int round = 0; round < 4; round++) { Thread.sleep(1_100); // let the once-a-second LRU clock move for (String k : hot) redis.get(k); // read the hot keys: they are young again int written = 0; String error = null; for (int i = 0; i < 800; i++) { try { redis.set("cold:" + round + ":" + i, value); written++; } catch (JedisDataException e) { error = e.getMessage(); break; } } System.out.printf("batch %d: wrote %d cold keys%s%n", round + 1, written, error == null ? "" : ", then: " + error); if (error != null) break; } long hotLeft = hot.stream().filter(redis::exists).count(); StringBuilder cold = new StringBuilder(); for (int round = 0; round < 4; round++) { int left = 0; for (int i = 0; i < 800; i++) if (redis.exists("cold:" + round + ":" + i)) left++; cold.append(round == 0 ? "" : ", ").append(left); } System.out.println("hot keys left: " + hotLeft + " of 200"); System.out.println("cold keys left per batch: " + cold); System.out.println("evicted_keys: " + (stat(redis, "stats", "evicted_keys") - evictedBefore) + ", used_memory: " + stat(redis, "memory", "used_memory")); } } static long stat(RedisClient redis, String section, String field) { for (String line : redis.info(section).split("\r\n")) { if (line.startsWith(field + ":")) return Long.parseLong(line.substring(field.length() + 1).trim()); } throw new IllegalArgumentException(field); } }

try.expect: Every policy except volatile-lru writes all four batches and evicts about 1,050 to 1,150 keys. allkeys-lru keeps hot keys left: 200 of 200, and the cold batches look like 103, 453, 800, 800 or 127, 335, 800, 800: the oldest batch goes first, but not all of it, because LRU here is sampled. allkeys-random keeps only about 120 hot keys (121 in my run) and spreads the losses evenly, 509, 519, 530, 676. allkeys-lfu keeps all 200 hot keys and evicts cold keys from every batch alike (460, 491, 470, 638): every cold key was used once, so they all tie. OBJECT FREQ hot:1 printed 6 or 7, while a cold key prints 5, the starting value. On a policy that isn't LFU, OBJECT FREQ fails with ERR An LFU maxmemory policy is not selected. volatile-lru behaves exactly like noeviction: an OOM error in batch 3 and evicted_keys: 0.

refs.title: Key eviction: approximated LRU and LFU
antirez: Random notes on improving the Redis LRU algorithm

analogy: Redis is a small library with one librarian. Some books carry a return-by date. The librarian sets no alarms. When someone asks for a book, she checks its date first, and if it has passed she takes the book away and says it isn't there. Ten times an hour she also walks to a few shelves and pulls out books whose date has passed, more shelves if she keeps finding them, but never for more than a quarter of the hour. When the shelves are full and a new book arrives, either she refuses it (noeviction) or she grabs five books at random and removes the one nobody has opened for longest. The analogy breaks on speed and on chance: a real librarian would spot an overdue book right next to the one she pulled, while Redis's sample really is random, and it repeats the whole routine thousands of times a second.
world: In a payment service, one Redis often ends up holding two kinds of data that want opposite settings. Idempotency keys and rate-limit counters are data: losing one means a duplicate charge or a broken limit, so they need a TTL on every key, noeviction, and an alert when used_memory gets near maxmemory. A cache of card-issuer BIN lookups or merchant profiles may lose anything at any time, so it wants allkeys-lru and no alert, because eviction is its normal state. Run them as separate instances with separate settings. Then size the data one: keys alive equals write rate times TTL. At 35 payments a second and a 24-hour TTL that is about 3 million keys. On the lab server 100,000 idempotency keys with a short JSON result took 16.7 MB (167 bytes each, though MEMORY USAGE reports 126 for one of them), so 3 million need about 500 MB before any headroom.
mistake: The most common mistake is running a Redis on the defaults: no maxmemory, so even noeviction never triggers, and the process grows until the container's memory limit kills it and every client loses its connection at once. The second is the reverse: setting allkeys-lru on the instance that also holds idempotency keys, sessions or locks. Under memory pressure, Redis evicts whatever has been idle longest, and a 23-hour-old idempotency key is exactly that, so the next retry of that payment finds no key and charges the card again. Both happen because defaults feel safe and one shared Redis feels simple. Decide per instance: data gets a maxmemory, noeviction and an alert; a cache gets a maxmemory and allkeys-lru.

compare.title: A TTL that survives the update, in Java and Kotlin

java.title: IdempotencyKeys.java
java.html: // a new payment request: claim its idempotency key for 24 hours, only if nobody has String claimed = redis.set(key, "pending", SetParams.setParams().nx().ex(86_400)); if (claimed == null) { return Outcome.DUPLICATE; // SET NX returns null when the key exists } // ... authorize with the issuer ... // record the result, but keep the deadline set above redis.set(key, "done:" + paymentId, SetParams.setParams().xx().keepTtl()); long secondsLeft = redis.ttl(key); // still about 86,400, not -1

kotlin.title: IdempotencyKeys.kt
kotlin.html: // a new payment request: claim its idempotency key for 24 hours, only if nobody has val claimed: String? = redis.set(key, "pending", SetParams.setParams().nx().ex(86_400)) if (claimed == null) { return Outcome.DUPLICATE // SET NX returns null when the key exists } // ... authorize with the issuer ... // record the result, but keep the deadline set above redis.set(key, "done:$paymentId", SetParams.setParams().xx().keepTtl()) val secondsLeft = redis.ttl(key) // still about 86,400, not -1

compare.note: The Redis commands are the same: SET ... NX EX 86400 to claim the key, then SET ... XX KEEPTTL to record the result without losing the deadline. Leave out keepTtl() and the second SET silently makes the key permanent, which is exactly the leak that TTL returning -1 reveals. Kotlin must declare claimed as String?: Jedis returns null when NX finds the key already there, and a platform type would let that null slip into code that expects a value. Lesson 8 builds the full idempotency flow on this.

Choose the settings. This is data, so noeviction. Set maxmemory with room above the steady state (here 1 GB) and the container limit with room above maxmemory for fragmentation, buffers and saves. Both are plain config lines.

lab.title: Build sampled LRU, then fill a real Redis under three policies
steps: Run the tests from the labs folder. All 13 fail: seven in SampledLruTest, a model that needs no Docker, and six in EvictionProbeTest, which start their own small Redis with maxmemory 4mb (the shared test server keeps its default settings).

In SampledLru.java, write chooseVictim: sample samples keys at random and return the one with the smallest lastUsed, or scan every key when the sample would cover them all. The storage and its helpers are done for you.

Write access: tick the clock, stamp a hit, or evict and insert on a miss. Run ./gradlew :redis:test --tests 'sfz.cache.l05.SampledLruTest'. Read the last two tests: 5 samples keep a hot set almost as well as exact LRU, and 1 sample is plain random eviction.
In EvictionProbe.kt, write fill, touch and stat. fill must stop at the first OOM error and say how far it got.
Run all 13 tests. The test allkeys-lru keeps the keys you keep reading takes about 5 seconds, because it waits for Redis's once-a-second LRU clock between batches.
hints: Sampling: keys.get(random.nextInt(keys.size())), samples times, keeping the candidate with the smallest lastUsed.get(...). Sampling with repeats is fine.
In access, check lastUsed.containsKey(key) for a hit. On a miss, evict before you insert, and only when keys.size() >= capacity.
Jedis throws redis.clients.jedis.exceptions.JedisDataException for the OOM error. Check e.message?.startsWith("OOM") == true, and rethrow anything else.

drill.title: Write chooseVictim from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. Given List<String> keys, Map<String, Long> lastUsed, int samples and a Random random, write String chooseVictim() the way Redis approximates LRU. Then compare. Why does Redis sample at all instead of keeping keys in order of use?

answer.html: String chooseVictim() { String victim = null; for (int i = 0; i < samples; i++) { String candidate = keys.get(random.nextInt(keys.size())); // a random key, O(1) if (victim == null || lastUsed.get(candidate) < lastUsed.get(victim)) { victim = candidate; // the oldest of the sample so far } } return victim; }

alt.html: fun chooseVictim(): String = (1..samples) .map { keys[random.nextInt(keys.size)] } // a random key, O(1) .minBy { lastUsed.getValue(it) } // the oldest of the sample

recap: A TTL is an absolute deadline stored with the key. A plain SET drops it; KEEPTTL keeps it; INCR and HSET leave it alone.

Expired keys are deleted lazily when touched, and by a cycle that checks 20 keys at a time, 10 times a second, in slices of at most 25 ms. An expired key is invisible at once but can sit in memory for a while: 500,000 keys took about 1.1 seconds to reclaim.
maxmemory defaults to no limit. The default policy, noeviction, refuses writes when full and keeps every key.

Eviction policies bet on recency (LRU), frequency (LFU) or both (ARC, W-TinyLFU). S3-FIFO and SIEVE drop one-hit wonders quickly and move nothing on a hit; SIEVE missed about 19% less than LRU in this lesson's demo.

Redis samples 5 keys into a pool of 16 and evicts the one idle longest (LRU), used least (LFU) or written least recently (LRM, 8.6). Use noeviction for data and allkeys-lru for a cache, in separate instances; volatile-* acts like noeviction when no key has a TTL.

explain.prompt: A teammate set EX 86400 on idempotency keys and is surprised that DBSIZE sometimes counts keys whose 24 hours are up, and that writes started failing once the instance filled up. Explain both, and what you'd change.
explain.answer: Redis doesn't delete a key at its deadline. Every command that touches a key checks the deadline first and deletes it then, so no client ever reads an expired key. Keys nobody touches are removed by a cycle that runs 10 times a second and checks 20 keys with a TTL at a time, going on while it keeps finding expired ones, for at most 25 ms per run. Until that cycle reaches a key, it still takes memory and still counts in DBSIZE. The failing writes come from the eviction policy. At maxmemory the default, noeviction, refuses writes instead of deleting anything. For idempotency keys that is right, because losing one could charge a card twice. So I'd keep noeviction, size maxmemory for write rate times TTL with room to spare, alert when used_memory passes 80% of it, and move any cache data to a separate instance with allkeys-lru.

deeper.html:
The active cycle has a second, faster mode. Before the event loop goes back to sleep, Redis may run a "fast" expiry cycle that lasts at most 1 ms. It runs only when Redis estimates that at least 10% of the keys with a TTL are already expired, or when the last slow run hit its time limit. The slow cycle in the 10-times-a-second timer does the bulk of the work. active-expire-effort (1 to 10, default 1) raises the batch size, the time budget and the acceptable stale share together: at 10, each batch checks 65 keys, a run may use 43% of the tick, and the cycle keeps going until only 1% of a batch is expired.

The freeing itself happens on the main thread unless you say otherwise. lazyfree-lazy-expire yes hands expired values to the bio_lazy_free background thread from lesson 2, and lazyfree-lazy-eviction yes does the same for evicted keys. That matters when keys are big: expiring one hash with a million fields frees a lot of memory in one go.

The 24-bit LRU stamp counts seconds and wraps after 2^24 seconds, about 194 days. Redis handles the wrap when it computes idle time, so a key idle for longer than that just looks less idle than it is. OBJECT IDLETIME shows the idle time in seconds, which is why it rarely shows anything but small numbers on a busy key.

One surprise while testing the eviction lab: a Lua script is checked against maxmemory only when it starts. If the server was over the limit then, the script's first write fails. Once a script has written anything, Redis lets it run to the end, because stopping it halfway would break its atomicity (the Transactions track's lesson on serial execution). A script that began under the limit wrote 100,000 keys of 1 KB into a server with maxmemory 4mb, and used_memory ended at 108 MB. A client that loops over SET sees the OOM error on time; one script can blow straight through the limit.

maxmemory-eviction-tenacity (default 10) limits how long one command may spend evicting before Redis moves the rest of the work to a background timer, so a burst of big writes can't stall one client for long. Set maxmemory-clients if a few clients with huge buffers could crowd out the data.

The papers behind the last section are short and readable. ARC's adaptation is a single number, the target size of the recency list, nudged up when a key evicted from the recency side comes back and down when one from the frequency side does. W-TinyLFU's sketch ages by halving every counter after a fixed number of additions, which is how it forgets yesterday's hot keys, and Caffeine tunes the size of its window by hill climbing while it runs. S3-FIFO's ghost queue holds only the names of as many keys as the main queue, so a key that was demoted too early gets a second chance without costing a slot. Twitter's study of its own caches found that plain FIFO did about as well as LRU for many workloads at the sizes they actually ran, and LRU pulled ahead mainly when a cache was too small.
